title: Disorders of the Synapse: Built, Then Kept

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What three roles can a synapse gene have across circuit development and adulthood?
cards.back: It can help build a circuit, keep it running, or do both.
cards.quote: A synapse gene can be needed to build a circuit, to keep it running, or both.
cards.section: Built wrong, or not kept running?

cards.front: Restoring a missing synapse gene in adult mice restores movement; deleting it in previously typical adults impairs movement. What does this establish about adult function, and what remains unknown about development?
cards.back: The adult circuit needs the gene, and movement can recover at the tested age. The late-test rules support upkeep but leave a building role open; rescue does not establish normal development.
cards.quote: Neither result rules out a role in building, and a failed rescue means little until you check that the gene really came back.
cards.section: Built wrong, or not kept running?

cards.front: A synapse gene is needed only to build a circuit. It is effectively deleted after that circuit is built. What happens to circuit function, and why?
cards.back: Function should persist: the completed circuit no longer needs this build-only gene.
cards.quote: Deleting a build-only gene late does nothing because the circuit is already built and no longer needs it.
cards.section: Built wrong, or not kept running?

cards.front: Adult restoration of a missing synapse gene produces no recovery. Before inferring an irreversible developmental defect, what must be checked about restoration?
cards.back: Check that the gene returned in enough cells, at the right level, and for long enough. Failure without those checks cannot establish irreversibility.
cards.why: Even adequate restoration may fail if secondary damage prevents recovery.
cards.quote: the gene did not come back in enough cells, at the right level, or for long enough
cards.section: Built wrong, or not kept running?

cards.front: Which two behavioural domains define autism spectrum disorder under DSM-5?
cards.back: Differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive behaviours and interests, present from early childhood.
cards.quote: differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive behaviours and interests, present from early childhood.
cards.section: What autism is, and why these two syndromes

cards.front: Why does an autism heritability estimate of roughly 60–90% not describe the genetic share of one person’s autism?
cards.back: Heritability describes how variation in diagnosis across a population tracks genetic variation; it does not divide an individual’s autism into genetic and other shares.
cards.quote: That is a population measure: across a population, most of the variation in who is diagnosed tracks genetic variation.
cards.section: What autism is, and why these two syndromes

cards.front: How do common variants and rare mutations differ in their contributions to autism?
cards.back: Many common variants with tiny effects likely supply most genetic contribution. Rare mutations contribute less overall, but one can have a large effect in an individual.
cards.quote: Most of the genetic contribution is thought to come from many common variants, each with a tiny effect
cards.section: What autism is, and why these two syndromes

cards.front: What three neuronal jobs are shared points of convergence for many autism-linked genes?
cards.back: Building and holding synapses, setting how much protein synapses make, and setting which genes neurons express.
cards.quote: Two large groups stand out, synaptic proteins and regulators of chromatin and transcription, and a theme links several others, giving three jobs.
cards.section: Three jobs, one meeting point

cards.front: SHANK3 holds receptors in the postsynaptic density as a {{c1::scaffold}} protein.
cards.back: The postsynaptic density lies under the receiving membrane of excitatory synapses.
cards.quote: SHANK3 is a scaffold protein that holds receptors in the postsynaptic density
cards.section: Three jobs, one meeting point

cards.front: How do TSC1, TSC2 and PTEN mutations converge on the same output affected by loss of FMRP?
cards.back: They raise mTOR activity, increasing protein synthesis; loss of FMRP removes a brake on synaptic protein synthesis.
cards.quote: TSC1, TSC2 and PTEN mutations all raise the activity of mTOR, a master regulator of protein synthesis
cards.section: Three jobs, one meeting point

cards.front: In the cortex, most inhibition comes from local interneurons that release {{c1::GABA}}.
cards.back: These interneurons make up about a fifth of cortical neurons.
cards.quote: In the cortex most inhibition comes from interneurons, local neurons that release GABA
cards.section: From synapse to circuit: excitation and inhibition

cards.front: A mature neuron loses excitatory receptors while its inhibitory input and other firing properties stay fixed. What happens to its response to the same excitatory input, and why?
cards.back: It should be less strongly driven toward firing: fewer excitatory receptors weaken the excitatory contribution relative to inhibition.
cards.quote: a synapse either excites the next neuron, pushing it toward firing, or inhibits it, holding it back.
cards.section: From synapse to circuit: excitation and inhibition

cards.front: Why can altered excitation–inhibition balance not be summarized as excess excitation in every autism model?
cards.back: The direction varies with brain region, cell type, age and model. No single imbalance explains autism.
cards.quote: Its direction differs between brain regions, cell types and ages, and between models, and no single imbalance explains autism.
cards.section: From synapse to circuit: excitation and inhibition

cards.front: How does a large CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 usually lead to loss of FMRP?
cards.back: Above about 200 copies, the control region usually becomes methylated, silencing FMR1 so little or no FMRP is made.
cards.quote: Above about 200 copies, the gene's control region usually becomes methylated and the gene is silenced, so little or no FMRP is made.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: An FMR1 CGG repeat count between about {{c1::55 and 200}} copies is a premutation.
cards.back: It can grow when a mother passes it on.
cards.quote: Between about 55 and 200 copies is a premutation, which can grow when a mother passes it on.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: What does FMRP normally do to the translation of many synaptic-protein mRNAs?
cards.back: It binds RNA and restrains translation, acting as a brake on local protein synthesis.
cards.quote: In neurons it travels with hundreds of mRNAs, many encoding synaptic proteins, and holds back their translation.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: Translation is blocked during induction of group I mGluR-dependent LTD in typical hippocampal tissue. What happens to lasting synaptic weakening, and why?
cards.back: The weakening does not last: normal mGluR-LTD requires new protein synthesis.
cards.quote: Normally this mGluR-LTD needs new protein: block translation, and the weakening does not last.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: Why is mGluR-LTD exaggerated and independent of fresh protein synthesis in Fmr1 knockout mice?
cards.back: The usual interpretation is that loss of FMRP leaves the needed proteins already in excess, allowing larger weakening without waiting for new synthesis.
cards.quote: the proteins it depends on are already there in excess, so the weakening is larger and need not wait.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: Halving mGluR5 in Fmr1 knockout mice moves protein synthesis toward typical levels. Does this prove excess mGluR5 activity originally caused the defect?
cards.back: No. The dosage rescue shows a genetic interaction; lowering mGluR5 could affect the causal route or compensate through another route.
cards.quote: A dosage rescue shows that the two genes interact; mGluR5 may be part of the cause
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: In a hypothetical translation assay, typical slices incorporate 100 units of labelled amino acid, slices lacking a translation brake incorporate 135, and an added receptor reduction lowers this to 102. What percentage of the excess above typical is removed?
cards.back: Initial excess = 135 − 100 = 35 units. Removed excess = 135 − 102 = 33 units. Percentage removed = (33/35) × 100 ≈ 94%.
cards.quote: Several traits moved toward those of typical mice, including protein synthesis
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: A lifelong reduction of mGluR5 improves traits in Fmr1 knockout mice. Design a comparison that tests whether reducing mGluR5 after symptoms begin can also help.
cards.back: Compare symptomatic adult knockout mice receiving an mGluR5 blocker with matched untreated knockout mice, measuring the same traits. The late-test rule requires a late intervention; a reduction present throughout development cannot answer this timing question.
cards.quote: because the halving was bred in, it was present throughout development, so it does not say whether lowering mGluR5 later would help.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: An animal circuit is unusually excitable. A drug strengthens GABA-mediated inhibition without changing excitation. What should happen to its tendency to trigger seizures, and why?
cards.back: The tendency should decrease: stronger inhibition can offset excess excitability. This predicts compensation, not proof that deficient inhibition caused the original defect.
cards.quote: Drugs that activate GABA receptors, which strengthen inhibition, reduce those seizures.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: An mGluR5 blocker corrects several traits in adult Fmr1 knockout mice but does not replace FMRP. What timing conclusion is supported, and which is not?
cards.back: Those traits remain adjustable in adult mouse circuits. The result does not establish when FMRP itself is needed, because the drug does not restore FMRP.
cards.quote: Because the drug does not put FMRP back, this does not say when FMRP itself is needed.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: A drug improves mouse traits but shows no benefit over placebo on the main human behavioural outcomes. What does this establish about transfer between species?
cards.back: The mouse improvement did not transfer to benefit for those drugs and measures. The negative trials alone do not establish why transfer failed.
cards.quote: The theory still explains a great deal of mouse biology, but it has not yet transferred to a treatment.
cards.section: Fragile X: a synapse that makes too much protein

cards.front: Mutations in {{c1::MECP2}} cause most cases of Rett syndrome.
cards.back: MECP2 encodes methyl-CpG-binding protein 2, MeCP2.
cards.quote: found that mutations in MECP2 cause most cases.
cards.section: Rett syndrome: a circuit that needs MeCP2 to keep running

cards.front: How is MeCP2 thought to regulate gene expression in neurons?
cards.back: It helps set expression levels of many genes, often by recruiting a co-repressor complex, rather than simply switching a few genes on or off.
cards.quote: is thought to help set the level at which many genes are expressed, often by recruiting a co-repressor complex
cards.section: Rett syndrome: a circuit that needs MeCP2 to keep running

cards.front: Why is a girl with one mutant MECP2 copy a mosaic of neurons with different active copies?
cards.back: Random X-inactivation leaves some neurons using the working MECP2 copy and others using the mutant copy.
cards.quote: some neurons use the working copy and others the mutant one.
cards.section: Rett syndrome: a circuit that needs MeCP2 to keep running

cards.front: Why do boys with severe MECP2 mutations usually have a different early course from girls with typical Rett syndrome?
cards.back: Boys have no working copy and usually have a severe course from early infancy; girls with one mutant copy retain a mosaic of cells using the working copy.
cards.quote: Boys with a severe mutation have no working copy and usually have a different, severe course from early infancy.
cards.section: Rett syndrome: a circuit that needs MeCP2 to keep running

cards.front: A new mutation occurs on a father’s X chromosome in a sperm cell. If that sperm produces a child, which sex receives this paternal X, and why?
cards.back: A daughter receives it: a father passes his X chromosome only to daughters.
cards.quote: a father passes his X only to daughters, so his new mutations land in girls.
cards.section: Rett syndrome: a circuit that needs MeCP2 to keep running

cards.front: Symptomatic adult mice regain MeCP2 after treatment and recover many symptoms. Why does recovery challenge an irreversible-miswiring explanation for those symptoms?
cards.back: The circuits can function once MeCP2 returns, so the recovered symptoms were not irreversibly fixed by development. This does not establish that development was normal.
cards.quote: the circuits were not irreversibly miswired: they could work once MeCP2 returned.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A drug switches a silent neuronal gene back on, and adult movement improves. What control helps distinguish gene restoration from an effect of the drug itself?
cards.back: Give the drug to mice without the switchable silent allele and measure movement. Improvement restricted to the restoration group supports gene-dependent recovery. The restoration rule requires that recovery depend on the gene returning, not merely on drug exposure.
cards.quote: the improvement should depend on the gene coming back, not on the drug.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What does deleting Mecp2 in previously typical adult mice add to the interpretation of adult MeCP2 rescue?
cards.back: Adult deletion causes symptoms, directly showing that the adult circuit still needs MeCP2. Rescue alone shows reversibility; neither test excludes a building role.
cards.quote: Both late tests point the same way: the adult circuit still needs MeCP2, though a role in building is not ruled out.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A treatment strengthens GABA signalling in the brainstem of Mecp2-deficient mice and reduces breathing pauses. Does that establish correction of their forebrain circuit imbalance, and why?
cards.back: No. The brainstem tends toward excess excitation, whereas the forebrain tends to be underactive. A regional benefit cannot establish correction elsewhere.
cards.quote: One gene, opposite imbalances, depending on the region.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What observation shows that more MeCP2 is not always better when considering replacement therapy?
cards.back: MECP2 duplication causes a separate syndrome in males; excessive MeCP2 is harmful.
cards.quote: Too much MeCP2 is harmful: duplication of MECP2 causes a separate syndrome in males.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A treatment restores neuronal function and reduces repetitive grooming in mice. Why do these combined findings still not demonstrate a treatment for human autism?
cards.back: The model-limit rule applies to both findings: circuit rescue tests a mouse mechanism, and grooming measures mouse behaviour. Together they establish neither the same causal step in human autism nor human treatment benefit.
cards.quote: A mouse rescue tests a mechanism, not a cure: it shows what a gene does in a mouse circuit at a given age.
cards.section: What mouse models can and cannot show

cards.front: What kind of evidence links some maternal infections during pregnancy to autism in children?
cards.back: Association, which alone does not establish causation. Most children of mothers with infections are not autistic.
cards.quote: These are associations, and most children of mothers with infections are not autistic.
cards.section: What mouse models can and cannot show

cards.front: Why does a negative mGluR5-blocker trial in young children weaken age at treatment as the explanation for earlier negative fragile X trials?
cards.back: Starting younger also failed to show benefit, so late treatment alone is a weaker explanation; the reason for failure remains unsettled.
cards.quote: Age at treatment was one proposed reason, but the negative trial in young children makes it a weaker explanation.
cards.section: Why the fragile X trials may have failed

cards.front: Why can a depolarizing GABA-A response still inhibit firing in an immature neuron?
cards.back: It can inhibit by shunting other inputs; depolarization alone does not establish increased firing.
cards.quote: depolarizing GABA can still inhibit firing by shunting other inputs.
cards.section: More on circuit balance

cards.front: In mice, removing MeCP2 only from somatostatin interneurons produces seizures with typical memory and social behaviour; removing it only from parvalbumin interneurons produces cognitive deficits without seizures. What does this imply for reading a whole-brain imbalance?
cards.back: Cell type matters as well as region. By the circuit-balance rule, one molecular defect can affect different circuit functions differently; a whole-brain label cannot identify the affected cell population or predict every trait.
cards.quote: In Rett models the cell type matters as much as the region
cards.section: More on circuit balance

cards.front: Adult Shank3 restoration in Shank3 mice improves grooming and social traits but not anxiety or motor coordination. Why is it inaccurate to call the entire syndrome either reversible or irreversible?
cards.back: Reversibility is trait-specific at the tested age: some traits recover and others do not. Nonrecovery alone does not establish a build-only requirement.
cards.quote: the late tests are read trait by trait: for one gene, some traits can still be reversed at an adult age and others could not be
cards.section: Each trait has its own window

cards.front: In a toy MeCP2 model, half the cells start at normal level 1 and half at 0. Vector copies per cell follow Poisson(m = 1); each adds 1. The allowed range is 0.5 ≤ level < 2. What fraction of cells is in range?
cards.back: Initially normal cells need 0 copies; initially deficient cells need exactly 1. P(0) = e⁻¹ and P(1) = e⁻¹. Fraction = 0.5P(0) + 0.5P(1) = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368 (36.8%), below the no-vector fraction of 50%.
cards.quote: A cell counts as in range from half the normal level up to, but not including, twice it, the duplication level.
cards.section: A dose window, worked

cards.front: What does poly(I:C) mimic in maternal immune activation experiments in mice?
cards.back: A viral infection: this synthetic double-stranded RNA triggers an immune response without a virus being present.
cards.quote: poly(I:C), a synthetic double-stranded RNA, mimics a viral infection and sets off an immune response with no virus present.
cards.section: Maternal immune activation in mice

cards.front: In pregnant mice, IL-6 alone produces offspring behavioural changes like those after immune activation, and blocking IL-6 prevents those changes. What causal role is supported, and what human claim remains unsupported?
cards.back: IL-6 is sufficient to produce similar changes and required for those changes in the tested mouse model. The model-limit rule prevents inferring that a cytokine causes autism in a child.
cards.quote: a single dose of the cytokine IL-6 had a similar effect, and blocking IL-6 prevented it.
cards.section: Maternal immune activation in mice

cards.front: A registry study links first-trimester hospital admission for viral infection to a roughly threefold autism diagnosis rate, with an imprecise estimate and no link across pregnancy overall. Can this establish a universal causal effect of maternal infection?
cards.back: No. The association rule does not establish causation; the result concerns a specific exposure window with imprecise evidence. It cannot be generalized to all maternal infections or all pregnancy stages.
cards.quote: though the estimate was imprecise and infection across pregnancy as a whole showed no link.
cards.section: Maternal infection in people

cards.front: Why should offspring behavioural changes after prenatal immune or antibody exposure in rhesus monkeys be interpreted cautiously?
cards.back: The studies used small animal samples. Altered monkey behaviour alone does not establish a cause of human autism.
cards.quote: These studies used small numbers of animals and need cautious reading.
cards.section: Monkeys and maternal antibodies
